items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: And there was another boy, a black boy, that played trumpet and saxophone... his name was Emmet Malone. He was a very good arranger and everything.

ctx.x: I want to ask you a question here. So then the music became a catalyst that was more important than the racial barrier ‘cause he had something you wanted to learn and you had something he wanted to learn.

That’s right, that’s true. And we got along fine because then I was playing alto, and he taught me how to transpose, he taught me a lot of things. And there was another boy, a black boy, that played trumpet and saxophone, but he loved carnivals and minstrel shows, and every time, if we didn’t lock him up when the minstrel show come to town he’d be gone, you know, and his name was Emmet Malone. He was a very good arranger and everything. I don’t know where he got the musical knowledge from, it was just sort of…

Let me ask you this. You mentioned this other player, you mentioned his tone, and you said you liked his tone. Would you consider that you also have a signature tone, where people can just hear your tone and know that’s you? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-
